33 CommentsFour of Wales' leading constitutional experts say they want to see the evidence behind Prime Minister Andy Burnham's rejection of calls for more powers to be transferred to Wales.

Writing to First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth last week, Burnham said he was "not persuaded" by the case for devolving policing and justice, the Crown Estate and rail infrastructure.

Prof Laura McAllister, Sir Paul Silk, Lord Thomas of Cwmgiedd and Lord (Rowan) Williams of Oystermouth led major reviews of Wales' constitutional arrangements.

In a letter to The Times, they say Burnham provided no "evidence-based counter argument" against further Welsh devolution.

Ap Iorwerth, Plaid Cymru's leader, said he was "deeply disappointed" that Burnham "does not view Wales as an equal nation".

It followed talks between the Labour prime minister and first minister in Glasgow in October that had previously been described as positive.

At Prime Minister's Questions, on Wednesday,  Burnham insisted he was "listening to Wales" and would "never completely rule things out".

But he told MPs he wanted to focus on devolving employment support, where he said there was "common ground" between the Welsh and UK governments.

He was replying to Plaid Cymru MP Ann Davies, who asked him: "When exactly did you decide Wales is no longer worth listening to?"

Image source, WPA Pool/Getty ImagesImage caption, Recent talks between the prime minister and first minister were described as positive

In their letter, published on Thursday, McAllister, Sir Paul, Lord Thomas and Lord Williams said their commissions had "engaged widely with the people of Wales and with experts, professional bodies and practitioners".

"That allowed us to accumulate compelling evidence that led to our conclusions that there should be further legislative devolution to Wales.

"And we received no credible evidence and no persuasive analysis to the contrary, certainly not from any Whitehall department.

"We were therefore perplexed and disappointed by the prime minister's letter last Friday to the first minister."

The four said devolving justice and rail would bring "real practical benefits" to Wales, adding that Burnham had offered no "evidence-based counter argument" against further devolution.

"We would dearly like to see the evidence that we were wrong," they wrote.

They concluded: "We urge the prime minister not to close a door and to remain open to evidence and persuasion."

The four were involved in three major reviews of Wales' constitutional arrangements: the Silk Commission on devolution, the Commission on Justice in Wales and the Independent Commission on the Constitutional Future of Wales.
